title: Kenya discharges last Ebola patient in major milestone towards virus-free status
content:
Kenya has discharged its last Ebola patient - the seventh to recover from the virus - marking a major milestone in efforts to contain the disease in the East African nation, which now begins a 42-day countdown to officially being declared Ebola-free.
It had confirmed its first ever case of Ebola early in October when a Kenyan businessman died within days of arriving in the capital, Nairobi.
He had contracted the virus in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where more than 5,000 people have died in an ongoing outbreak that began in May. His mother also subsequently died.
Kenya's health minister said 135 identified contacts of the infected patients had also completed their 21 days in isolation.
"Today with the discharge of the last patient we can confirm and tell the world that seven patients have recovered - and all contacts have completed their follow-up monitoring," Aden Duale said.
The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) described it as an important achievement in the regional response to the outbreak.
"This is an encouraging moment for Kenya and for Africa. We must sustain surveillance and vigilance until the outbreak is officially declared over," Africa CDC chief Jean Kaseya posted on X.
Kenya has reported no new confirmed cases since 20 October.
All the Kenyan cases were linked to the man who had travelled from DR Congo through Uganda, with health officials reporting no evidence of wider community transmission.
Those who have recovered following treatment included four healthcare workers.
Five patients were discharged on 3 November, followed by a sixth three days later, before the final patient was cleared on Wednesday.
Under World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines, 42 days must pass after the last patient tests negative and is discharged, or the last Ebola victim is safely buried, before an outbreak can be declared over.
The Ebola virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit. The incubation period ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks.
Duale said the government would maintain heightened surveillance at border crossings, airports, health facilities and communities throughout the countdown.
Emergency response teams will remain on alert across the country, while the health authorities will continue monitoring travellers arriving from affected countries.
Kenyans returning from Ebola-affected areas are required to complete electronic health declarations before travelling, undergo screening on arrival and spend 21 days in quarantine under the supervision of health teams.
The minister also urged countries that had imposed travel and visa restrictions to reconsider them - adding that Kenya had no intention of serving as a quarantine centre for another country.
In May, a Kenyan court suspended US plans to open an Ebola quarantine facility for American citizens.
Kenya has maintained that there is no need to restrict domestic travel, trade or public gatherings.
The outbreak has nevertheless disrupted international travel, with some Gulf countries introducing restrictions affecting travellers from Kenya and other African countries.

title: Adults think kids are more creative than they are, but new research shows that’s not the case
content: Emily Liu’s 2-year-old daughter, Rose, writes piano melodies, makes up yoga moves and turns mixing bowls and pacifiers into hats and jewelry. She makes up her own recipes too, although consumers should be wary of rocks. “Nobody’s told her it’s supposed to be done a certain way, or supposed to look a certain way,” said Liu, who lives in Atlanta. “Creativity stems from that kind of autonomy, independence and innocence that comes with being a young child.” Many people share Liu’s sentiment that kids are more creative than adults. But new research suggests that they might just be more confident in their creativity. The study , published recently in PLOS One, found that adults aren’t less creative than preschoolers. In fact, grownups had more novel and effective ideas while completing creative tasks. However, preschoolers demonstrated more self-confidence and enthusiasm about the activities — particularly those without constraints or goals. “Even if you’re a super creative thinker, you might not actually show it if you don’t feel encouraged, or if you’re fearful that your ideas might get rejected,” said study coauthor Mathias Benedek, a researcher at the University of Graz in Austria. Researchers assigned 92 children and 70 adults three tasks: drawing a mythological creature, finding unique uses for a tin can, and drawing anything they wanted. Their work was evaluated based on novelty, effectiveness and overall creativity. Adults scored higher than children across the three criteria, especially when given the tin can and mythological creature tasks with specific goals . The results indicate that creativity thrives under greater cognitive and metacognitive control, Benedek said. Still, children reported a more positive experience throughout the tasks, indicating higher self-efficacy, motivation, enjoyment and self-appraisal. Adults reported higher anxiety that they wouldn’t perform well on the tasks. “Children really thrived when there was no clear goal — for example, the creative drawing task, they really liked that most,” Benedek said. “Adults didn’t feel comfortable when they had no clear goal in the task. They really wanted to understand what they were supposed to do.” At the beginning of the study, participants were asked whether they think children or adults are more creative. Children split evenly on the answer, while 78% of adults agreed that children are more creative. The results supported a pre-study survey, where 80% of adult respondents shared the same view. This might be because people perceive creativity differently, according to Maryam Abdullah, the parenting program director of the Greater Good Science Center at the University of California, Berkeley — relating it to “emotional or experiential creativity, rather than the actual sophistication of creativity.” Liu, who also has a 9-year-old son, tries to encourage her daughter’s creativity by asking open-ended questions and giving her independence. She agrees that children are more creative than adults. “There’s an innocence about them. They haven’t been impacted by society yet,” Liu said. “They’re not worried about social norms, they’re not worried about being judged or what the right way to do something is. They’re just doing what comes naturally to them.” This widespread impression that children are more creative — something Sandra Russ, a distinguished psychology professor at Case Western Reserve University, said most researchers would refute — was what Benedek said inspired the study in the first place. Russ, who authored a book about creativity and play, emphasized that parents and teachers giving children time and space for unstructured, independent activities is critical for fostering creativity. “If they want you to engage with them — draw with them, play with them — do it,” Russ said. “But let them make up the story, let them make up the drawing. Don’t interfere.” She said that for kids ages 4 through 9, creativity often manifests as pretend play with dolls, cars, building blocks or other toys. Once the preteen years hit, it becomes more cognitive: Creativity can mean daydreaming, making up a science project or approaching a math problem with a unique perspective. Abdullah added that one of the first steps to supporting children’s creativity is to notice and affirm it. She said that simply telling children that it’s valuable to think outside the box will encourage more creative behavior. “The study asks, ‘Are children really more creative than adults?’ And the findings answer that question,” Abdullah said. “But what it asks that’s more interesting is, ‘Are children creative more often than adults?’”

Researchers have identified another potential approach to treating pancreatic cancer, with early experiments suggesting that blocking a protein could slow tumor growth and strengthen immune defenses. Pancreatic tumors can be surrounded by tissue so dense that it compresses blood vessels, making it difficult for nutrients to reach cancer cells. Even under these conditions, the cells continue growing. How they obtain the materials needed to survive has remained an important question. Researchers at Fox Chase Cancer Center have identified one way pancreatic cancer cells obtain cholesterol and other fats, known as lipids. Their study, published in Nature Cancer , also identified a protein that helps control this process and could offer a potential target for cancer treatment. The research focused on pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), the most common type of pancreatic cancer. These tumors contain large numbers of cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), cells that produce and organize connective tissue. As CAFs and their collagen fibers expand, they can compress nearby blood vessels, restricting the tumor’s blood supply. Despite contributing to this nutrient shortage, CAFs also help cancer cells overcome it. “We found that CAFs can act as a source of these nutrients,” said Edna Cukierman, PhD, a professor and co-leader of the Cancer Signaling and Microenvironment Program at Fox Chase and co-senior author of the study. “Using laboratory and animal models, we discovered that CAF units acquire cholesterol from the bloodstream and transfer it to nearby pancreatic cancer cells through a process called trogocytosis” Trogocytosis occurs when one cell takes small pieces of another cell’s membrane during direct contact. In this case, pancreatic cancer cells acquire pieces of CAF membranes containing cholesterol and other lipids that support their survival and growth. The researchers discovered that this transfer depends on a protein called anoctamin 6 (ANO6), which helps prepare the CAF membrane for the exchange. “These findings help explain how pancreatic cancer cells obtain essential nutrients despite the unusual structure of the pancreatic tumor microenvironment,” said Igor Astsaturov, MD, PhD, a professor at Fox Chase and co-senior author of the study. “Cancer-associated fibroblasts are not passive bystanders. They actively support tumor growth by transferring lipids to cancer cells.” When researchers reduced or eliminated ANO6 in CAFs, the cells became less effective at supporting pancreatic cancer cell survival. In mouse models, tumors supported by CAFs with functional ANO6 grew substantially faster than those without functional ANO6. The same nutrient transfer process also appeared to interfere with the immune system. Cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) are immune cells that recognize and kill cancer cells. When these T cells come into contact with CAFs, they can acquire membrane material containing cholesterol. Excess cholesterol in the tumor environment can contribute to T-cell exhaustion, making these immune cells less effective at fighting cancer. “With Serge Fuchs, professor at the University of Pennsylvania and co-author on the paper, we were surprised to find that the same cellular mechanism can benefit the tumor in two ways – by supplying cancer cells with lipids while also weakening cancer-fighting T cells,” said Astsaturov. “Targeting ANO6 could potentially disrupt both of these tumor-supporting functions at the same time.” In mouse models, blocking ANO6 reduced cholesterol accumulation in T cells within tumors and improved markers of their activity. Laboratory experiments also showed that T cells exposed to CAFs with reduced ANO6 were better able to kill cancer cells. The researchers then tested whether drugs that interfere with ANO6-dependent activity could slow tumor growth. In mouse models, treatment with niclosamide or clofazimine significantly reduced tumor weight. Niclosamide also reduced cholesterol delivery to pancreatic cancer cells. These findings suggest that targeting ANO6 could both restrict a nutrient source for pancreatic tumors and improve the immune response against them. However, the results remain preclinical, and further research is needed to determine whether selectively blocking ANO6 would work as a treatment in patients. Trogocytosis is also only one of several ways pancreatic cancer cells may obtain lipids. The researchers suggest that the drugs tested could potentially help treat other difficult cancers, although that possibility requires further investigation. “We believe our findings identify ANO6 as a potential therapeutic target that could simultaneously disrupt the nutrient supply supporting pancreatic cancer cells and reduce the immune-suppressive effects of the tumor microenvironment,” said Astsaturov. The findings also build on nearly a decade of research into how the tissue surrounding pancreatic tumors supports cancer growth. “Excitingly, reducing ANO6 expression also disrupted the stromal synapse-mimicry circuit we previously identified, which coordinates tumor nutritional support, CAF-unit metabolism, and immune suppression. These findings position ANO6 as the missing mechanistic link that unifies nearly a decade of discoveries by our team,” said Cukierman.
